analysis.one_liner: Bans BPA in food and drink containers and forces safety retesting of food-contact chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban BPA in food containers was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 2013-2015 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell food in any container made with or releasing bisphenol A (BPA), the chemical long used in the linings of metal food and drink cans and in hard plastic containers. Companies that could prove no workable substitute exists could get a one-year, renewable waiver, but would have to put a BPA warning on the label. It would also require the Food and Drug Administration to re-review chemicals already approved for food packaging, weighing low-dose exposure and effects on pregnant women, infants, and children, and require makers of food-packaging chemicals to submit safety findings before their products enter commerce.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats canned or packaged food, especially pregnant women, infants, and children, who would face less exposure to BPA, a chemical that can mimic estrogen. States, tribes, and localities could keep stricter rules of their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially pregnant women and children

how_it_helps.text: Treats food sold in containers containing or releasing BPA as adulterated — the same legal category as food containing poison — 180 days after passage [S2, S3].

Lets the Health and Human Services Secretary grant one-year renewable waivers only where no substitute is technologically feasible, and requires a prominent BPA warning label on any waived product [S2, S3].

Requires FDA to set a schedule for re-reviewing approved food additives and packaging chemicals, considering low-dose effects and vulnerable groups, with mandatory remedial action when a chemical fails the safety standard [S2, S3].

Requires manufacturers of food-contact substances to notify the government before use that their chemical shows no low-dose harm and no reproductive or developmental toxicity in appropriate tests [S2, S3].
Preserves the right of states, localities, and Indian tribes to adopt or enforce stricter BPA rules and warnings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical and packaging companies that produce BPA and food and beverage companies that use epoxy-lined cans would bear the cost of switching to alternatives, or of waiver paperwork and warning labels during the transition.

drawbacks.text: Food and beverage companies would face real switching costs; the waiver process exists precisely because some containers may not have feasible BPA-free alternatives at the time of the ban [S2, S3].
The waiver mechanism would allow BPA use to continue indefinitely in one-year increments as long as a substitute remains infeasible, with only a label as protection for those products [S2, S3].

At the time, the FDA's own position was that low levels of BPA in food were safe, and in 2012 it had banned BPA only in baby bottles and sippy cups rather than across the food supply; industry argued the evidence for harm at typical exposure levels was unproven. A full ban went beyond what federal regulators were then willing to do.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health rationale — reducing exposure of pregnant women, infants, and children to a synthetic estrogen mimic — is the bill's core strength, and the re-review of packaging chemicals is a structural fix to a system that approves chemicals with little post-market checking. The costs are real but modest by packaging-industry standards: many major can makers were already moving to BPA-free linings under consumer pressure, and the waiver-plus-label system softens the transition. The main honest criticism is scientific — regulators were not convinced that typical exposure levels cause harm — though the bill's defenders would answer that the review provisions are designed to settle that question with evidence.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a markup or a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Representative Edward Markey introduced the bill on June 4, 2013, joined by 21 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1, S3, S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S1, S5].
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where the record ends — no further action appears in the bill's history [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a House floor vote, or companion action that produced law during the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that make or use BPA in food and beverage containers are better off: no federal ban was enacted, so canned and packaged goods could keep using BPA-based linings during this Congress, and consumers continued bearing whatever exposure risk the sponsors feared.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ban Poisonous Additives Act of 2013 and led its introduction.

for.name: 21 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or consideration after referring it to the Health Subcommittee; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were House Democrats; the Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: A ban on BPA in food containers would remove their largest food-packaging market, since BPA-based epoxy is the standard lining inside metal cans. Their interest in continuing sales ran directly against the bill's goal of reducing consumer exposure.

industries.industry: Food and beverage canners and packaged-food companies
industries.note: They would face reformulation, waiver, and labeling costs, but many were already shifting to BPA-free linings under consumer pressure, and the bill's waiver system limits how fast they must change. Consumers get lower exposure in exchange for whatever costs are passed through.

industries.industry: Makers of alternative food packaging and safety testing firms
industries.note: A mandate to find substitutes and a new regime of pre-market safety notifications would create demand for alternative packaging materials and toxicology testing.
